passages.happening:
Jesus finishes instructing the twelve and goes on to teach and preach in the towns of Galilee. Meanwhile John the Baptist is in prison. Matthew will tell later how he got there: Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, arrested him for condemning his marriage (14:3-4).

In his cell John hears about what Jesus is doing. He sends his own disciples to ask a question: “Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?”

Jesus does not answer yes or no. He tells them to go back and report what they hear and see: “The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor.” Then he adds one more line for John: “Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.”
passages.hearers:
This is the same John who had preached by the Jordan and baptized Jesus. He had said that one more powerful than he was coming, with a winnowing fork in his hand, to gather the wheat and “burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (3:11-12). Now that one had come. But what John heard about was healing, teaching, and meals with tax collectors. The fire had not fallen. And John was still in a king's prison.

The Jewish historian Josephus, writing near the end of the first century, also tells of John's arrest. He says John was held and put to death at Machaerus, a palace fortress east of the Dead Sea.

‘The One who was to come’ was a way of speaking about the one God had promised to send. Jews in Jesus' day did not all hope for the same figure. Some longed for a king from David's family, some for a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), some for Elijah to return before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5). A broken scroll found in a cave at Qumran, by the Dead Sea, and known as 4Q521, says that when God's anointed one comes the Lord will heal the wounded, make the dead live, and bring good news to the poor (some translate ‘the meek’). Scholars debate whether that scroll means God does these works himself or through his anointed one. Either way, Jesus' list matched what some Jews were hoping to see.

The words ‘fall away’ translate the Greek verb skandalizō. A skandalon was the trigger of a trap or a stone that trips you up. Jesus is saying: happy is the one who does not trip over me because I am not what he expected.
passages.ot:
Jesus' answer is woven out of Isaiah. Isaiah promised a day when “the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped” and “the lame will leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:5-6). He promised that “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19). And the one anointed by God's Spirit would “preach good news to the poor” (Isaiah 61:1).

Notice what Jesus leaves out. The same passages also speak of judgment. Isaiah 35:4 says “your God will come with vengeance,” and Isaiah 61:2 speaks of “the day of our God's vengeance.” Jesus quotes the mercy and not the vengeance. Judgment is still coming in Matthew (11:22-24 is only a few verses away). But mercy comes first. That may be exactly what puzzled John.
passages.hard:
Did John doubt? He had seen the Spirit come down on Jesus (3:16). How could he now ask whether Jesus was the one?

Christians have read it two ways. John Chrysostom, a preacher of the late 300s, argued that John did not doubt at all. He sent his disciples for their sake, so they would see Jesus' works for themselves and follow him. Many modern readers think the question was real. John had pictured the coming one bringing judgment, and what he heard did not fit. A prison cell is also a dark place to think in. Both readings are held.

What is plain is how Jesus treats the question. He does not scold John. He sends him evidence, the things people could see and hear, and a gentle blessing. Then, as soon as the messengers leave, he praises John in front of the crowd (verses 7 to 11). Doubt in a faithful person is not the same as unbelief. John took his question to the right place.

If you are a believer who doubts, or you are in a dark place yourself, this passage is in the Bible for you. You may bring your question to Jesus as John did. And if the darkness is heavy and does not lift, please talk to someone who can help: a pastor, a doctor, or a crisis line. Getting help is not a failure of faith.
passages.asks: John did not hide his question or pretend he had none. He sent it straight to Jesus. Ask what you do with your own questions about God: bury them, walk away with them, or bring them to him? And look at Jesus' answer. Where can you see what he is doing, even if it does not look the way you expected?

passages.happening:
As John's disciples leave, Jesus turns to the crowd and speaks about John. He asks three questions. When you went out into the wilderness, what did you go to see? A reed swaying in the wind? A man dressed in fine clothes? Those live in palaces. A prophet? “Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.”

John is the messenger the Scriptures promised, sent ahead to prepare the way. No one born of a woman has been greater than John. “Yet even the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.”

Then come two harder sayings. Since John began, the kingdom of heaven “has been subject to violence, and the violent lay claim to it.” All the Prophets and the Law pointed forward until John. And, Jesus says, “if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who was to come.” He ends with a call to listen: “He who has ears, let him hear.”
passages.hearers:
Crowds had walked out to the Jordan to hear John (3:5). Jesus reminds them what they found. Reeds grew thick along the river. A reed in the wind bends whichever way the breeze blows. John was not like that. He had told a ruler to his face that his marriage was wrong, and he was in prison for it.

Some scholars have noticed something else. Coins struck by Herod Antipas around AD 19 or 20, for his new city of Tiberias, carry a picture of a reed. They suggest the crowd might have thought of Antipas himself, the ruler who bent. Others call this a clever guess, since no ancient source says people called Antipas a reed.

‘Fine clothes’ belonged in kings' palaces. John wore camel's hair and a leather belt (3:4). He was in a king's palace now, but in its prison.

‘The least in the kingdom is greater than he’ does not mean John is shut out. It means John stood at the edge of something new. He pointed to Jesus but died before the cross and the empty tomb. The humblest follower who has seen those things stands in a better place to understand than even John did.
passages.ot:
Jesus quotes the prophet Malachi: “Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me” (Malachi 3:1). In Malachi, the LORD is speaking, and the messenger prepares the way for God himself. Jesus applies it to John preparing the way for him.

Malachi's last words promise more: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD” (Malachi 4:5). Jesus says John is that Elijah. Yet in John's Gospel, when asked “Are you Elijah?” John answers, “I am not” (John 1:21). The two fit together. John was not Elijah come back from heaven. He came, as the angel told his father, “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). That is why Jesus adds ‘if you are willing to accept it’.
passages.hard:
What does verse 12 mean? The kingdom “has been subject to violence, and the violent lay claim to it.”

The Greek verb, biazetai, can be read two ways, and the noun for ‘the violent’ can mean attackers or simply forceful, eager people. One reading, which the Berean Standard Bible follows, takes it as a complaint: since John began preaching, the kingdom has been under attack. Herod has locked John up, and the leaders will soon plot to kill Jesus (12:14). Violent people try to seize or crush God's work.

A second reading takes it as praise: the kingdom is breaking in with power, and eager people press into it. Luke's version of the saying sounds that way: “everyone is forcing his way into it” (Luke 16:16). Many preachers have read it as a call to seek God with all your strength. A third reading holds both: because the kingdom comes with power, it meets fierce resistance.

Careful scholars still differ, and these notes do not settle it. All the readings agree on the main point of verse 13. John marks a turning point. The time of promise is ending, and the time of fulfilment has come.
passages.asks: Jesus asks the crowd three times, ‘What did you go out to see?’ Ask yourself the same. When you go to church, open the Bible, or listen to a preacher, what are you hoping for: something comfortable, something impressive, or the truth even when it costs? John was none of the first two. He was the third.

passages.happening:
Jesus compares his generation to children sitting in the marketplace and calling to their friends: “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.”

John came fasting, and people said, ‘He has a demon.’ Jesus came eating and drinking, and they said, “Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!” Then Jesus answers them: “But wisdom is vindicated by her actions.”
passages.hearers:
Anyone who has watched children play knows this scene. In the open square of a town, children played at grown-up life. Sometimes it was a wedding, with a pipe and dancing. Sometimes it was a funeral, with a sad song and mourning. And there were always some children who would not join any game. Too happy for the funeral, too sulky for the wedding.

That is how people had treated God's messengers. John was strict. He lived in the wilderness and fasted, so they said he was mad, possessed by a demon. Jesus went to dinners and ate with anyone, so they said he was a party-goer who kept bad company. The complaints point in opposite directions. The real problem was not John's fasting or Jesus' feasting. It was that people did not want to hear either of them.

‘Vindicated’ means proved right. In Matthew's Greek, ‘actions’ is erga, ‘works’, the same word as ‘the works of Christ’ in verse 2. The deeds of Jesus will show in the end whose wisdom was true. Luke gives the saying as “wisdom is vindicated by all her children” (Luke 7:35).
passages.ot:
‘Glutton and drunkard’ were not light words. They come from the Law, where parents bring a rebellious son before the elders of the town and say, “He is a glutton and a drunkard” (Deuteronomy 21:20). In the Law that son faced death. To call Jesus this was to call him a disgrace to his people.

The figure of Wisdom also stands behind verse 19. In Proverbs, Wisdom is pictured as a woman who calls out in the streets and sets a table, inviting the simple: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed” (Proverbs 9:5). Jesus, the friend who eats with sinners, is doing what Wisdom does. The chapter will end with his own invitation (11:28).
passages.asks: Some people will find a reason to refuse any messenger: too strict, too loose, too serious, too joyful. Ask whether your objections to God are reasons or excuses. If God sent you exactly the messenger you asked for, would you listen then?

passages.t: Woe to the towns that did not turn
passages.happening:
Jesus begins to denounce the towns where most of his miracles had been done, because they did not repent. “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!” If the same miracles had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. On the day of judgment it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon than for them.

Then he turns to his own base, Capernaum. “And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades!” If Sodom had seen these miracles, it would still be standing. On the day of judgment it will be more bearable for Sodom than for Capernaum.
passages.hearers:
‘Woe’ is a prophet's cry. It is not a curse spoken with glee. It is closer to ‘alas’: grief and warning mixed together.

The three towns were near neighbours on the north side of the Sea of Galilee. Chorazin lay in the hills about two miles north of Capernaum. It is named in the Bible only here and in Luke 10:13. Visitors today see ruins of black basalt stone, including a synagogue, but most of what stands dates from well after Jesus' time, and the town he knew has not yet been uncovered. Bethsaida was the home town of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44), though scholars still argue over exactly where it stood. Capernaum was where Jesus lived after leaving Nazareth (4:13). These were the places that had seen the most.

Now listen to the comparisons. Tyre and Sidon were rich Gentile ports on the coast to the north-west, and the prophets had condemned their pride (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26 to 28). Sodom was the city God destroyed in Genesis 19, the byword for wickedness. For a Jewish town to be told that pagan Tyre and wicked Sodom would do better on the day of judgment was shocking.

Sackcloth was rough cloth, worn with ashes on the head as a sign of grief and repentance. When Jonah preached in Nineveh, its king “covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes” (Jonah 3:6). Hades is the Greek name for the place of the dead, like the Hebrew Sheol.
passages.ot:
The words to Capernaum echo Isaiah's taunt against the proud king of Babylon, who said in his heart, “I will ascend to the heavens” and was told, “But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit” (Isaiah 14:13, 15). A small fishing town that had Jesus living in it was in danger of the same pride.

Sodom's sin is named in Ezekiel: “She and her daughters were arrogant, overfed, and complacent; they did not help the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49). In the same chapter the prophet tells Jerusalem that it has done worse than Sodom. Jesus speaks in that prophetic line.
passages.hard:
Jesus says Tyre and Sidon would have repented if they had seen these miracles. Then why were the miracles not done there? And is it fair to judge anyone for what they were never shown?

Christians have answered in different ways, and these notes do not choose between them. Some, who stress God's free choosing, say God owes grace to no one. Tyre and Sidon are judged for their own sins, and the saying is mainly about the guilt of the Galilean towns that saw so much and still did not turn. Other Christian thinkers have built on this verse the idea that God knows what free people would do in every possible situation, and orders history with that knowledge in mind. Many readers of every tradition add that this is the strong language of a prophet, like Ezekiel saying Jerusalem was worse than Sodom. Its point is the responsibility of those who have seen, not a map of what might have been.

Whatever else is said, the text itself gives a word of fairness. ‘More bearable’ means judgment is not the same for everyone. It is measured by the light a people were given. Those who never saw are not judged as those who saw and turned away.
passages.asks: These towns did not reject Jesus with anger. They simply got used to him. The miracles became part of the scenery. Ask whether that has happened to you. Repentance, the word these towns refused, is not a feeling of being sorry. It is turning around. Is there something you have heard from God many times and never turned toward?

passages.t: Hidden from the wise, shown to little children
passages.happening:
Right after the woes, Jesus prays aloud: “I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight.”

Then he says something about himself that is among the boldest words in the Gospels: “All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father. No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.”
passages.hearers:
‘These things’ means what Jesus' works were showing: that the kingdom had come and who he was. ‘The wise and learned’ would make Jesus' hearers think of the experts in the Law, the people everyone expected to understand first. ‘Little children’ is the Greek nēpioi, infants. It points to the fishermen, tax collectors and ordinary people who were following Jesus.

This is not praise of ignorance. Jesus is not against learning. The point is how the gift is received. A small child does not earn what a parent gives. It simply receives. Cleverness can become a wall, and a person who thinks he already knows may never ask.

To ‘know’ in the Bible is more than having facts. It means a close, personal knowing. Jesus claims that he and the Father know each other in a way no one else does, and that others come to know the Father through him. These words sound very like John's Gospel, where Jesus says, “just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father” (John 10:15). Early Christians drew on passages like these when they confessed that the Son shares the Father's very being.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament often says that God's wisdom confounds human wisdom. Through Isaiah God warned, “The wisdom of the wise will vanish” (Isaiah 29:14). Daniel praised the God who “reveals the deep and hidden things” (Daniel 2:22). And a psalm says, “From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise” (Psalm 8:2), a verse Jesus will quote when children praise him in the temple (21:16).

‘All things have been entrusted to Me’ looks ahead to the end of Matthew, where the risen Jesus says, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me” (28:18).
passages.hard:
Does God choose to hide himself from some and show himself to others? Verse 25 says the Father has ‘hidden’ these things, and verse 27 says the Son reveals the Father to those he ‘chooses’.

Christians have read this in different ways for centuries. Those who stress God's choosing say that knowing God is always his free gift. No one finds him by being clever, and no one can boast. Those who stress human response point to the setting. The towns just named were proud and would not turn, and God hides himself from people who think they have no need of him while he shows himself to the humble. They also point to the very next verse, which invites ‘all’ who are weary.

Both sides agree on a great deal. No one reaches God by brains or rank. The gift is received with empty hands. And the invitation that follows is open to anyone who will come. These notes leave the deeper question where faithful Christians have left it, open for discussion and not a cause for division.
passages.asks: Ask whether you come to God more like an expert or more like a child. Knowledge of the Bible is good, and these notes exist to help you gain it. But it can also become a way of keeping God at arm's length. What would it look like to receive from him today, instead of trying to master him?

passages.t: Come to Me: the easy yoke
passages.happening:
Then Jesus turns from prayer to invitation. These three verses are found only in Matthew:

“Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.”
passages.hearers:
A yoke was a wooden beam laid across the necks of two working animals, such as oxen, so they could pull a plough or cart together. Everyone in a farming village knew what one looked like. It was also a common picture for being under someone's rule. When King Rehoboam wanted to threaten his people, he said, “I will add to your yoke” (1 Kings 12:11).

Jewish writers also used the yoke as a picture of taking on God's teaching and living by it. Rabbinic writings from after Jesus' time, written down from around AD 200 onwards, speak of reciting the Shema, Israel's daily confession that the LORD is one, as taking on ‘the yoke of the kingdom of heaven’.

Early in the second century BC, about two centuries before Jesus, a Jewish teacher in Jerusalem named Ben Sira wrote a book of wisdom, called Sirach or Ecclesiasticus. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include it; Protestant Bibles do not count it as Scripture. Near its end he invites the untaught to come to his school, to put their necks under Wisdom's yoke, and he says that he himself laboured only a little and found much rest (Sirach 51:23-27, in summary). Jesus' words sound very like this. But notice the difference. He does not say ‘take Wisdom's yoke’ or ‘take the Law's yoke’. He says ‘take My yoke’ and ‘learn from Me’. He puts himself in the place of God's Wisdom.

‘Weary and burdened’ would include people worn out by hard work and poverty, and people weighed down by religion. Later Jesus will say of some teachers that “They tie up heavy, burdensome loads and lay them on men's shoulders” (23:4). His word for ‘gentle’ is praus, the same word as ‘the meek’ in 5:5 and the king who comes ‘gentle and riding on a donkey’ in 21:5.
passages.ot:
The words ‘you will find rest for your souls’ are taken straight from Jeremiah. God told his people, “Stand at the crossroads and look. Ask for the ancient paths: ‘Where is the good way?’ Then walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls.” But the people answered that they would not walk in it (Jeremiah 6:16). Jesus offers the same rest, and this time it is found by walking with him.

Rest is a promise God made from the start. To Moses he said, “My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest” (Exodus 33:14). And the Sabbath, God's weekly gift of rest, is the subject of the very next chapter. Matthew sets the invitation to rest right before the arguments about the day of rest.
passages.hard:
How can Jesus call his yoke easy? He also says “take up his cross” (10:38) and gives the hard teaching of the Sermon on the Mount. Following him is not light work.

The word for ‘easy’ is chrēstos, which also means good or kind. Some readers picture a yoke shaped well, so that it does not rub. Jesus is not promising that there will be no load. He promises that his load fits, and that you do not carry it alone. A yoke is made for two. The one beside you is ‘gentle and humble in heart’.

Many people have heard this invitation as one more demand: try harder, pray more, do better. Read it again. It is not a demand. It is an invitation from a person: come to me. If you are worn out, by grief, by guilt, by caring for someone, or by a kind of religion that felt like a weight you could never lift, these words are spoken to you. If you are afraid of God's judgment, this is the voice that speaks to you first.

Rest in Christ does not replace other help. If you are exhausted and it does not lift, or if weariness has turned into despair, please see a doctor or talk to a pastor or a crisis line. Weariness of body and mind can be illness, and getting care is not a lack of faith.
passages.asks: The first word is ‘Come’. Not ‘fix yourself first’. Ask what you are carrying right now, and whose yoke you are under: other people's expectations, the need to prove yourself, an old guilt. Then hear the invitation as it is given, to you, by name. What would it mean to bring that load to him today?
